courses.description: Students will examine how democratic systems function (and sometimes falter) at the local, state and national levels. Through a combination of seminar discussions, deliberation exercises, guest speakers and experiential learning opportunities - including field trips to Richmond and Washington, DC, local government meetings and community forums - students will explore the real-world mechanics that civic leaders must navigate to make democracy work. As part of a residential learning community, students will engage in collaborative projects, practice deliberative dialogue in their residence halls and develop the civic skills necessary for meaningful participation in American democracy. By the end of the semester, students will not only understand the machinery of democratic governance but also see themselves as active contributors to its ongoing maintenance and improvement.
courses.title: Mechanics of Democracy for Civic Leadership

courses.description: Addressing growing cynicism and distrust in government today calls for active citizen civic leaders. Framed and guided by James Madison's legacy, civic leadership involves learning key skills to foster collaboration across differences, embracing complexity in decision making and in dialogue with others, and valuing pragmatic solutions that advance the common good. In many ways, this is the antithesis of what we see from contemporary national political leaders, making this class important for students wanting to engage deeply and meaningfully improve the civic health and participation of their communities.
courses.title: Civic Leadership: Theories and Practice

courses.description: Working with the civic leadership minor coordinator and a faculty advisor, students will complete a 3-6 credit civically engaged leadership internship and report. The internship is designed to provide an academic context for performing and analyzing off-campus work in government, public service, and non-profit settings. Utilizing knowledge, theories, dialogue, and collaboration methods and skills gained in CIV 300 , students will assess and reflect on their internship experience in real time by writing weekly structured reflections.
courses.rawPrerequisiteText: Prerequisites: CIV 300 and permission of the instructor. Corequisites: CIV 300 .

courses.description: A study of the law as a means of social, political and economic change. The course focuses on the law in positive leadership development and organizational success. The course has two main goals: To develop leaders who are able to achieve success by understanding the legal and ethical aspects of their business responsibilities and to show how organizations can achieve competitive advantage by reducing legal risk and using the law to create economic value, while also encouraging responsible conduct. The course examines legal and ethical issues that every businessperson should understand to make sound business decisions in a global environment. courses.description: This course is an exploration of dance as an art form. It emphasizes learning about and experiencing a broad spectrum of dance forms through lecture, discussion, movement exploration, and attending and viewing dance performances. The course considers the historic and cultural significance of dance as well as the components of a dance performance: dancers, choreographic elements, production design (costuming, lighting, scenic elements, etc.) and audience. The course reveals how dance has informed the human experience throughout history. It does this by placing dance's "embodied way of knowing" within social, artistic, religious, political and cultural contexts. It provides an opportunity for the student to experience an appreciation for the dynamic, varied and complex role that dance has played in human societies over time, and understand how it relates to other art forms. courses.rawPrerequisiteText: Prerequisites: Applied to Teacher Education (01 Flag); a minimum grade of "C" in ECED 372 . Corequisites: ECED 443 , ECED 445 and LED 456 .

Candidates will examine and reflect on their personal attitudes, assumptions and behaviors toward students and their families who represent diverse class, cultural and linguistic backgrounds. Students will complete 80 hours over the course of the full semester (16 weeks).

courses.title: Mathematics Content and Pedagogy for Early Childhood Education I

Emphasis is on children's mathematical learning of geometry, measurement, data analysis and probability.

courses.title: Mathematics Content and Pedagogy for Early Childhood Education II

courses.description: This all-day, primary-grade practicum allows students to demonstrate their educational decision-making skills through planning, implementing and evaluating appropriate activities for children of diverse interests, needs and abilities. Strategies to assess learning, guide behavior, work with professionals and involve families are applied in this practicum and accompanying seminar.

courses.title: Integrated Day Practicum

courses.description: Enables students to apply in public school classrooms those understandings, skills and attitudes acquired in all components of teacher education. Under the guidance of university supervisors and cooperating teachers, students engage in full-time teaching responsibilities.

May be used for general education credit.

courses.title: Contemporary Economic Issues and Policy Alternatives

courses.description: A survey of the relationships among national economies, including trade theory, trade policy, international monetary relations and the balance of payments.

courses.title: International Economics

courses.description: Students will learn key mathematical and statistical concepts used in economics. Topics will include algebra of summation, optimization, probability theory, joint probability distribution, conditional expectations, hypothesis testing and an introduction to data analysis using statistical software. Concepts will be emphasized using economic examples. Does not count as COB 291 for COB 300.
courses.rawPrerequisiteText: Prerequisites: MATH 205 , MATH 231 , MATH 235 or equivalent; and either COB 191 , MATH 220 , MATH 318 or equivalent.
courses.title: Introduction to Quantitative Analysis in Economics 1,2

courses.description: An analysis of the problems of the environment, their causes and alternative proposed methods of solution. Air and water pollution will be stressed as case studies of environmental problems.
courses.rawPrerequisiteText: Prerequisites: ECON 201 .
courses.title: Environmental Economics

courses.description: Examines facts and theories pertaining to the various economic roles of women in America. The economics of marriage, divorce and childbearing are examined as are empirical and theoretical explanations of occupational and wage differentials between the sexes.
courses.rawPrerequisiteText: Prerequisites: ECON 201 .
courses.title: The Economics of Women and the Family

courses.description: An examination of the distinguishing characteristics, institutions and performances of the various types of major economic systems in the world today.
courses.rawPrerequisiteText: Prerequisites: ECON 200 and ECON 201 .
courses.title: Comparative Economic Systems

courses.description: Introduction to the field of public finance including theories and principles of taxation, government expenditure, public debt, and fiscal administration. Studies interrelationships between federal, state and local finance, shifting and incidence of tax, and the burden of public debt.
courses.rawPrerequisiteText: Prerequisites: ECON 200 and ECON 201 .
courses.title: Public Finance

courses.description: Examines interdependent decision making in economics and other social sciences, and covers both non-cooperative and cooperative games. Topics may include applications of game theory to industrial organization, law and economics, public choice, political economy, evolutionary biology, international affairs and theories of justice.
courses.rawPrerequisiteText: Prerequisites: ECON 200 and ECON 201 or permission of the instructor.
courses.title: Game Theory

courses.description: An introductory course in behavioral economics that combines insights from psychology with economics. Using data from field and lab experiments, we will examine the explanatory power of the standard economic model and learn new frameworks that incorporate psychologically realistic assumptions grounded in observed behavior. Among the topics studied are decision-making under uncertainty, intertemporal choice and others regarding preferences. The course will conclude by examining implications this approach to economic analysis has for public policy.
courses.rawPrerequisiteText: Prerequisites: ECON 201 .
courses.title: Behavioral Economics

courses.description: This course explores the structure, conduct, and performance of hospitals, physician practices, pharmaceutical and medical device manufacturers, and long-term care facilities. The demand for healthcare and insurance is presented using economic theories of risk and uncertainty. Economic evaluation of healthcare treatments and contemporary policies are examined.
courses.rawPrerequisiteText: Prerequisites: ECON 200 and ECON 201 .
courses.title: Health Economics

courses.description: Intermediate analysis of the determination of price, resource allocation and product distribution in a free enterprise economy.

courses.title: Intermediate Microeconomic Theory 3

courses.description: Intermediate-level analysis of the major approaches to the determination of economic aggregates, with emphasis given to structuring a common analytic framework.

courses.title: Intermediate Macroeconomic Theory 3

courses.title: Economics of Natural Resources

courses.description: Study of the economics of labor markets. Attention is given to the structure and operation of labor markets, wage determination, employment, unions, and contemporary labor problems and policies.

courses.title: Labor Economics

courses.description: A study of the characteristics of under-development, theories of economic development and the underlying causes for varying standards of living among the world's people. courses.rawPrerequisiteText: Prerequisites: ECON 200 and ECON 201 .
courses.title: Economic Development

courses.description: An examination of the classical and modern theories of international trade, the effects of such trade on the domestic economy, the effects of barriers to free trade and an appraisal of U.S. commercial policy since 1948.
courses.rawPrerequisiteText: Prerequisites: ECON 200 and ECON 201 .
courses.title: International Trade and Trade Policies

courses.description: Examines international financial markets, instruments and institutions; determination of spot and forward exchange rates, interest arbitrage, hedging and speculation; and alternative policies for achieving equilibrium in international payments.
courses.rawPrerequisiteText: Prerequisites: ECON 200 and ECON 201 .
courses.title: International Finance and Payments

courses.description: A detailed examination of the economic aspects of urbanization with emphasis on metropolitan land use and location theory. Urban problems considered include housing, poverty, labor markets and municipal finances.
courses.rawPrerequisiteText: Prerequisites: ECON 200 and ECON 201 .
courses.title: Urban Economics

courses.description: Course will provide basic mathematical tools for microeconomic and macroeconomic analysis. Topics covered include linear algebra, univariate and multivariate differentiation, economic interpretation of the derivatives, constrained and unconstrained optimization, expected utility model, and dynamic analysis of economic models.

courses.title: Mathematical Economics

courses.description: This course covers the application of single- and multi-variable linear regression models to economic outcomes, with emphasis on hypothesis testing, causal effect estimation and data analyses using statistical software.

courses.title: Econometrics

courses.rawPrerequisiteText: Prerequisites: ECON 200 and ECON 201 .
courses.title: Economics Internship (topic must be related to Environment and Natural Resources)

courses.description: Evaluation and critique of mainstream and nontraditional economic paradigms. The interaction of economics and politics in the United States as it affects the distribution of wealth and domestic and international economic policies.
courses.rawPrerequisiteText: Prerequisites: ECON 200 , ECON 201 , and junior or senior standing.
courses.title: Political Economy

courses.description: Examines the justification for and nature of public sector activity in a market-based mixed economy. Emphasis is placed on theories of market failure, voting models, conditions of production and provision in the public sector, and models of bureaucratic behavior.
courses.rawPrerequisiteText: Prerequisites: ECON 326 or ECON 331 .
courses.title: Theory of Public Choice

courses.description: This course focuses on using incentivized experiments, whereby subjects make financially-motivated decisions in controlled environments, to identify causality, test and develop theories, and explore behavioral phenomena related to economic issues. Students will study and apply the methods and data analysis tools commonly used in experimental economics to a broad range of economic topics. Established experimental results from previous and current economic research will also be thoroughly examined.
courses.rawPrerequisiteText: Prerequisites: ECON 327 or ECON 331 .
courses.title: Experimental Economics

courses.description: Examines alternative theories of the relationships between money, interest rates, price levels, employment and output in order to assess the effectiveness of monetary policy for economic stabilization.
courses.rawPrerequisiteText: Prerequisites: ECON 332 .
courses.title: Monetary Theory

courses.description: Examines theories of general equilibrium and the distribution of income, welfare economics, capital theory and information theory.
courses.rawPrerequisiteText: Prerequisites: ECON 331 .
courses.title: Advanced Microeconomic Theory

courses.description: This course studies macroeconomics at an advanced level. Topics covered in this course may include short-run dynamics of an economy, theory of economic fluctuations, models of long-run economic growth, role of fiscal and monetary policies, and comparative macroeconomic analysis of the U.S. and other economies.
courses.rawPrerequisiteText: Prerequisites: ECON 332 .
courses.title: Advanced Macroeconomics

courses.description: Economic growth is at the heart of economics: improving standards of living in the long run. Students will study models of economic growth, their applications and the empirical evidence across countries. Particular emphasis will be placed on recent advances in the area. Students will apply data analysis methods commonly used in economic growth to a broad range of topics.
courses.rawPrerequisiteText: Prerequisites: ECON 332 .
courses.title: Economic Growth

courses.description: A study of the rationale, methods and impact on industry behavior of government regulations including public utility regulation and antitrust policies relating to monopoly and competition in the United States.
courses.rawPrerequisiteText: Prerequisites: ECON 385 or permission of the instructor; and ECON 331 or ECON 345 (to use ECON 345 , students must have permission of the ECON 455 instructor).
courses.title: Economics of Regulated Industries

courses.description: A study of local and subnational economics viewed as integral parts of a unified system. Emphasis will be given to the basic economic forces associated with regional growth and decline and related public policy considerations.
courses.rawPrerequisiteText: Prerequisites: ECON 200 and ECON 201 .
courses.title: Regional Economics

courses.description: This is an advanced level class in Econometrics with an emphasis on time series techniques. This course covers a broad range of time series methods commonly used in research and industry for generating short-term forecasts for important economics and financial variables. Some of the topics covered are time series decomposition methods, smoothing methods, ARIMA, ARCH/GARCH and VAR.

courses.title: Applied Time Series Analysis 1

courses.description: Theory and application of statistical techniques to study empirical relationships among economic variables. This course will cover a range of econometric techniques to estimate economic models including panel data, limited dependent variable, and simultaneous equation models. In addition, the course will cover the assembly and analysis of requisite data sets, and the preparation and presentation of empirical results.
courses.rawPrerequisiteText: Prerequisites: Minimum grade of "B-" in ECON 385 .
courses.title: Advanced Econometrics 1

courses.description: This course is a writing-intensive seminar offering a student the opportunity to integrate many of their undergraduate studies in economics. Its substantive content will emphasize applying the methods of theoretical and empirical analyses employed by all economists. The seminar will be structured so as to contain embedded assessment measures of the learning objectives specified by the department of economics, including those related to command of basic economic theory and of quantitative methods used in quantifying empirical relationships and testing hypothesis.

courses.title: Senior Capstone Seminar in Economics

courses.description: Designed to give capable students in economics an opportunity to complete independent study under faculty supervision. Admission by recommendation of the instructor and written permission of the director of economics prior to registration. May not be used toward fulfillment of the 400-level requirement for a major in economics.
courses.title: Special Studies in Economics (topic must be related to Environment and Natural Resources)

courses.description: This course provides an overview of the U.S. American public education system. Specific emphasis will be placed on the role, funding and history of education as they relate to social justice, equity and the diversity of U.S. American society. May be used for general education credit.
courses.rawPrerequisiteText: Prerequisites: If you have already completed, or are currently registered for, a Critical Thinking (Madison Foundations) class, then you must secure permission to receive credit for a second Critical Thinking class.
courses.title: Critical Questions in Education [C1CT]

courses.description: This course examines development and sociocultural dynamics, informed by 21st century skills, with a retrospective focus on how past developmental experiences impact present and future learning. Students will apply knowledge and research about human development to identify best practices for learning and resilience. This course may be used for general education credit.
courses.title: Learning, Behavior and Engagement in Context [C5SD]

courses.description: This course addresses understanding of American education, philosophical approaches to education, the history of education, and the socio-cultural changes in U.S. society with characteristics of today's schools and with current educational issues.
courses.title: Foundations of Education in the United States

courses.description: This is an introductory course that examines the historical, sociological, philosophical, and psychological perspectives that influence and support the curricular and instructional structures of general education. Throughout the course the implementation of those structures through a systematic process of planning for effective classroom instruction and evaluation will be examined. Connections to how they reflect an understanding of various models of learning and cognition and their implications for educational practice will be established.

prerequisiteExpr.value: Minimum grade of " C" in requisites

courses.title: Foundations of Curriculum and Instruction

courses.description: This course engages students in critical studies of educational outcomes and practices for minority populations in contemporary and historical contexts.
courses.title: Critical Studies in Education, Race, Culture and Politics

courses.description: This course will examine how personal and professional values, attitudes, beliefs, and behaviors affect teaching and learning. The pre-service teachers will develop an understanding of similar unique characteristics of Pre-K to 12 grade students and their families, including culture, race, ethnicity, heritage language and learning abilities, gender socialization, and sexual orientation.
courses.title: Teaching in a Diverse Society

courses.description: This course offers an in-depth examination of selected topics which are of current importance in the field of education. This course may be repeated for credit when course content changes.
courses.rawPrerequisiteText: Prerequisites: Junior or senior standing and consent of the instructor.
courses.title: Special Topics in Education 2

courses.description: This course is an introduction to global issues shaping education policy and practice around the world. Students are invited to examine their own identities and actions and their implications for global issues at the local and transnational levels. Course readings, co-curricular activities and instruction are designed to promote an attainable global perspective in order to support the development of global competencies in future course taking and educational praxis. A portfolio of Global Education assignments, essays and curriculum materials will be established.
courses.rawPrerequisiteText: Prerequisites: Declared ELED Global Concentraiton.
courses.title: Introduction to Global Education

courses.description: Skills for observing, recording and interpreting the behavior of children ages three through 12 will be developed so that adult intervention and guidance is appropriate and meaningful.
courses.title: Child Development: Birth Through Adolescence

courses.description: This course will examine how personal and professional values, attitudes, beliefs and behaviors affect teaching and learning. The pre-service teachers will develop an understanding of unique characteristics of Pre-K to 12th grade students and their families, including culture, race, ethnicity, heritage, language, learning abilities, gender socialization and sexual orientation. In this globalized version of the course, students will also develop global competencies by examining local and global issues, engaging in open and critical conversations with oneself and others, and acting for collective well-being and sustainable development. The course integrates the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) to foster a deeper understanding of global challenges and their relevance to elementary education.
courses.rawPrerequisiteText: Prerequisites: Declared ELED global concentration and ELED 200 . Corequisite: ELED 272 and ELED 278 .
courses.title: Global Diversity in Elementary Education

courses.description: This course is designed to introduce elementary education students to teaching children in grades PK-6. Based on developmental and learning theories, the course focuses on building relationships with and among learners, establishing learning environments, guiding behavior, and providing instruction and assessment. Through observations and participation in practicum, seminars, workshops and lectures, students will construct an understanding of how teachers meet the developmental and learning needs of children by planning, implementing and assessing appropriate curriculum and instruction.
courses.rawPrerequisiteText: Prerequisites: ELED or B.I.S./ELED major: Teacher Ed flag 01. Corequisites: ELED majors: ELED 208 and ELED 310 , or ELED 270 and ELED 278 .
courses.title: Introduction to Early and Elementary Education

courses.description: This course introduces a lifespan approach to human growth and development with emphasis on the social, physical, emotional and cognitive domains. Students will examine key theories, educational philosophies and research methods in the social sciences and child development. They will also develop skills for observing, recording and interpreting children's behavior to apply appropriate and meaningful guidance. In addition, the course emphasizes the professional development of future educators by fostering reflective and culturally responsive practice. Global perspectives are integrated throughout the course, encouraging students to consider cultural diversity, environmental sustainability and global interconnectedness in their understanding of children's growth and learning. Students will also connect local classroom practices to broaden global citizenship values and strengthen cross-cultural competence as part of their preparation for teaching in diverse contexts.
courses.rawPrerequisiteText: Prerequisites: Declared ELED global concentration and ELED 200 . Corequisites: ELED 270 and ELED 272 .
courses.title: Child Development in a Global Context: Birth Through Adolescence

courses.description: This course will examine how personal and professional values, attitudes, beliefs and behaviors affect teaching and learning. The pre-service teachers will develop an understanding of unique characteristics of Pre-K to 12th grade students and their families, including culture, race, ethnicity, heritage, language, learning abilities, gender socialization and sexual orientation.
courses.rawPrerequisiteText: Prerequisites: ELED or B.I.S./ELED major. Corequisites: ELED majors: ELED 208 and ELED 272 .
courses.title: Diversity in Elementary Education

courses.description: This field experience, taken in the fall of junior year, provides candidates with a classroom of students and a mentor teacher with whom to practice building relationships with learners and conduct extensive observations of learners and learning, as well as practice the teaching of content related to their concurrent methods courses (either language arts, mathematics and science OR language arts, mathematics and social studies) with small groups of students. Accompanying monthly seminars will focus on reflecting on themes and experiences in the field and making content connections to methods courses.
courses.rawPrerequisiteText: Prerequisites: ELED or B.I.S./ELED major; Teacher Ed flag 02. ELED majors: ELED 272 . Corequisites: ELED majors: ELED 332 and ELED 333 , or ELED 372 and ELED 373 .
courses.title: Practicum with a Focus on Learners and Learning

courses.description: This field experience, taken in the spring of junior year, provides candidates with a classroom of students and a mentor teacher with whom to practice the teaching of content related to their concurrent methods courses (either language arts, mathematics and science OR language arts, mathematics and social studies) with small groups of students as well as in full class contexts. The accompanying monthly seminar explores the integration and construction of meaningful curriculum in elementary education contexts and in classroom management as well as reflection along with field-based partners.
courses.rawPrerequisiteText: Prerequisites: Accepted to teacher education.
courses.title: Practicum with a Focus on Curriculum Integration and Guiding Behavior

courses.description: This course is a study of content, processes, pedagogy and materials for teaching science in the elementary classroom. Knowledge of cognitive development as applied to the selection of content and methodology for elementary learners will be examined.
courses.rawPrerequisiteText: Prerequisites: ELED or B.I.S./ELED major. ELED majors: ELED 272 . Corequisites: ELED majors: ELED 321 , ELED 333 and LED 300 .
courses.title: Children and Science

courses.description: The first of two courses that provides students with knowledge, skills and understanding to design and implement effective, developmentally appropriate mathematics instruction for grades PreK-6. This course will focus on mathematical instruction connected the following mathematical strands: Number and number sense, computation and estimation, and patterns, functions and algebra.
courses.rawPrerequisiteText: Prerequisites: ELED 272 . Corequisites: ELED 321 , ELED 332 and LED 300 .
courses.title: Children and Mathematics I

courses.description: This course focuses on the content, processes, pedagogy and materials for teaching social studies in the elementary classroom. Knowledge of cognitive development as applied to the selection of content, methods, materials and strategies for organizing the learning environment for elementary learners will be examined.
courses.rawPrerequisiteText: Prerequisites: ELED or B.I.S./ELED major. ELED majors: ELED 321 and LED 300 . Corequisites: ELED majors: ELED 322 , ELED 343 and LED 350 .
courses.title: Children and Social Studies

courses.description: This is the second course in a series providing students with knowledge, skills and understanding to design and implement effective, developmentally appropriate mathematics instruction for grades PreK-6. Emphasis is on children's mathematical learning about geometry, measurement, data analysis and probability.
courses.rawPrerequisiteText: Prerequisites: ELED 321 and LED 300 . Corequisites: ELED 322 ; ELED 334 and LED 350 , or ELED 374 , ELED 375 and LED 370 .
courses.title: Children and Mathematics II

courses.description: This course is a study of content, processes, pedagogy and materials for teaching science in the elementary classroom. Knowledge of cognitive development as applied to the selection of content and methodology for elementary learners will be examined. Students explore methods for fostering scientific literacy within a global context, emphasizing interconnected challenges such as sustainability and public health. The course also examines diverse cultural perspectives on scientific knowledge and practices to create more inclusive classrooms.
courses.rawPrerequisiteText: Prerequisites: Declared ELED global concentration and ELED 272 . Corequisites: ELED 321 , ELED 373 and LED 300 .
courses.title: Children and Science in a Global Context

courses.description: This is the first of two courses that provides students with knowledge, skills and understanding to design and implement effective, developmentally appropriate mathematics instruction for grades PreK-6. This course will focus on mathematical instruction connected to the following mathematical strands: number and number sense, computation and estimation, and patterns, functions and algebra. In this globalized version of the course, students will also develop global competencies by examining how mathematics is taught differently around the world, and engaging in open and critical conversations with oneself and others to foster a deeper understanding of different mathematical strategies and how to teach them.
courses.rawPrerequisiteText: Prerequisites: Declared ELED global concentration and ELED 272 . Corequisites: ELED 321 , ELED 372 and LED 300 .
courses.title: Children and Mathematics I in a Global Context

courses.description: This course focuses on the content, processes, pedagogy and materials for teaching globally-aware social studies in the elementary classroom. Knowledge of cognitive development as applied to the selection of inclusive and global content, culturally sustaining methods, materials, and strategies for organizing the learning environment for elementary learners will be examined.
courses.rawPrerequisiteText: Prerequisites: Declared ELED global concentration, ELED 321 and LED 300 . Corequisites: ELED 322 , ELED 343 and LED 370 .
courses.title: Children and Social Studies in a Global Context

courses.description: In this course students will explore the needs and challenges of elementary school learners and reflect on what they've learned about teaching young children in a global context. Throughout the semester, students will be prompted to reflect on their experiences with teaching in a global context. Reflections will focus on understanding the complexities inherent in teaching as well as their own personal beliefs, strengths and areas for growth. Students will revisit and expand upon the portfolio begun in ELED 200 .
courses.rawPrerequisiteText: Prerequisites: Declared ELED global concentration, ELED 321 and LED 300 . Corequisites: ELED 322 , ELED 343 , ELED 374 and LED 370 .
courses.title: Seminar in Global Education Praxis I

courses.description: Upon completion of this course, teacher candidates will be able to build upon the unique strengths and contributions of K-6 students in order to create and teach lessons in various subject areas as well as reflect on that process.
courses.rawPrerequisiteText: Prerequisites: ELED or B.I.S./ELED major. ELED majors: ELED 322 and ELED 343 . Corequisites: ELED majors: ELED 480 .
courses.title: Elementary Education Final Practicum (taken twice for a total of 2 credits)

courses.description: This is the first of two courses that helps prospective elementary education teachers (PreK-6) develop mathematical content and pedagogical knowledge, skills and understanding to design and implement effective, developmentally appropriate mathematics instruction for grades PreK-6. Emphasis is on children's mathematical learning in the following mathematical strands: number and number sense, computation and estimation, and patterns, functions and algebra.
courses.rawPrerequisiteText: Prerequisites: Applied to Teacher Education (01 Flag).
courses.title: Mathematics Content and Pedagogy for Elementary Education I

courses.description: This is the second of two courses that helps prospective elementary teachers (PreK-6) develop mathematical content and pedagogical knowledge, skills and understanding to design and implement effective, developmentally appropriate mathematics instruction for grades PreK-6. Emphasis is on children's mathematical learning of geometry, measurement, data analysis and probability.
courses.rawPrerequisiteText: Prerequisites: Applied to Teacher Education (01 Flag); ELED 444 .
courses.title: Mathematics Content and Pedagogy for Elementary Education II

courses.description: Elementary education teacher candidates will learn the process of planning, implementing curriculum and using instructional strategies and assessments that promote and monitor students' understanding of content beyond memorization. Students will design units of instruction that utilize evidence-based practices for active engagement strategies, specifically for providing an inclusive environment for a diverse student population. Students will gain the knowledge and skills necessary to use assessments that allow for data-driven instructional decisions and inform subsequent teaching and learning.
courses.rawPrerequisiteText: Prerequisites: ELED or B.I.S./ELED major. ELED majors: ELED 322 and ELED 343 . Corequisites: ELED majors: ELED 485 .
courses.title: Planning Instruction and Assessment

courses.description: Study of the role of the teacher in relating to and working with families, school personnel and communities. Methods of involving stakeholders and providing effective communication among groups are emphasized. Resources for supporting parents and engaging community stakeholders are examined.
courses.rawPrerequisiteText: Prerequisites: ELED or B.I.S./ELED major. ELED majors: ELED 450 . Corequisites: ELED majors: LED 462 , or ELED 475 and LED 473 .
courses.title: Home, School, Communities

courses.description: In this course, students will explore challenges and opportunities in developing a globally focused praxis for teaching content and skills to diverse elementary school learners. Students will integrate learning in teaching placements with content from education courses taken in the ELED major. Throughout the semester, students will be prompted to reflect on their experiences with teaching in a global context. Reflections will focus on understanding the complexities of planning curricula that expand students' worldviews and promote critical global citizenship. Students will revisit and expand upon the portfolio begun in ELED 200 and expanded in ELED 375 .
courses.rawPrerequisiteText: Prerequisites: Declared ELED global concentration and ELED 450 . Corequisites: ELED 455 and LED 473 .
courses.title: Seminar in Global Education Praxis II

courses.description: This internship provides a context in which to demonstrate and integrate the skills, knowledge and dispositions that are essential for success as an elementary classroom teacher. Under the guidance of a university supervisor, students are expected to reflect on the teaching role as they assume the full responsibilities of a teacher in grades PreK-6. Students majoring in elementary education must complete this course twice for a total of 16 credit hours.
courses.rawPrerequisiteText: Prerequisites: ELED or B.I.S./ELED major; Teacher Ed flag 03. ELED majors: ELED 322 and ELED 343 . Corequisites: ELED majors: ELED 400 .
courses.title: Student Teaching in Elementary Education (taken twice for a total of 16 credits)

courses.description: This course presents an overview to classroom management for the early childhood and elementary classroom teacher. It includes an historical look at the guidance tradition, a review of traditional approaches to classroom management and a focus away from punishment toward proactive strategies. Best practices in classroom management will be presented from an inclusive perspective for teachers of all children.
courses.rawPrerequisiteText: Prerequisites: ELED or B.I.S./ELED major. ELED majors: ELED 322 and ELED 343 . Corequisites: ELED majors: ELED 450 . Also open to B.I.S./ELED majors.
courses.title: Guiding Student Behavior: Responsive Classroom Management

courses.description: Designed to give students opportunities to complete independent research on educational problems under faculty guidance. The plan for the study must be presented to the department head in prescribed form for approval prior to registration.

courses.description: This course will take a thematic approach to understanding and analyzing literature by examining multiple texts that engage with a common course theme or idea concerned with one or more aspects of human experience. This course will introduce students to methods for studying literature through thematically focused analysis. The organizing principle of this course will be thematic, but the course will also engage with form and the cultural aspects of the literature studied. This is a writing-infused course. Specific topics will vary. This course may be used for general education credit.
courses.title: Literature and Ideas [C2L]

courses.description: This course will take a genre-based or formalist approach to understanding and analyzing literature by examining multiple texts that belong to a genre, subgenre and/or other category of literary and/or artistic creation. This course will introduce students to methods for studying literature through analysis focused on the forms and conventions of the selected texts. The organizing principle of this course will be the analysis of literary form, but the course will also engage with the thematic and cultural aspects of the literature studied. This is a writing-infused course. Specific topics will vary. This course may be used for general education credit.
courses.title: Literature and Genres [C2L]

courses.description: This course will take a cultural and contextual approach to understanding and analyzing literature by examining multiple texts that develop from, represent or respond to human experiences of specific times, places, histories and/or identities. This course will introduce students to methods for studying literature through culturally and contextually focused analysis. The organizing principle for this course will be contextual analysis, but the course will also engage with form and the thematic aspects of the literature studied. This is a writing-infused course. Specific topics will vary.
courses.title: Literature and Cultures

courses.description: A general survey presented chronologically. May be used for general education credit.

Writing and revision will form central components of this course. Students will refine and apply their knowledge of specialized terms, concepts and critical methodologies for literary analysis. This course prepares students for upper-level work in literary studies.

Text studied may include fiction, poetry, drama, essays and memoirs written primarily, but not exclusively, in the 20th century.

It examines the colonial, nationalist and postcolonial shaping of individual and collective identities through literature; the intersections of race, gender and nation; the crafting of a new idiom in English in response to both political and literary histories; and the significance of choices of genre and form.
courses.title: Literature and Empire

courses.description: An introduction to the study of film as an aesthetic practice, including formal and industrial aspects of film analysis, theoretical approaches to film and writing and research methodologies of film and media studies.

courses.description: A historical and worldwide survey of major film movements from the silent era to the present-day, including Asian, European, African, American, Middle Eastern, Australasian and transnational cinemas. Focus will be placed on the aesthetics, politics and sociocultural contexts of global cinemas, with a focus on films that explore shifting ideologies and cultural identities in times of social tumult. Students will investigate how film movements worldwide respond to issues of geopolitics, globalization, colonization, nation-building, modernization, underdevelopment, migration and social marginalization.
courses.title: History of Global Cinemas

courses.description: This course explores specific topics within the study of race, class, gender and their intersections in national and/or global cinemas. The course uses key films and readings to introduce students to interrogate key historical and theoretical issues informing cinematic constructions of race, class and/or gender. The course will familiarize students with evolving discourses of racial, class and sexual identities in national and/or global cinemas, with a particular focus on the ways in which specific films and media industries reinforce and/or challenge dominant discourses on race, class and gender identity.
courses.title: Race, Class and Gender in Film

The course emphasizes processes associated with making evidence-based decisions in engineering fields. This course covers the following topics: processes of decision making, engineering documentation, data analysis, visualization and engineering orthographic drawing. Students are permitted a maximum of two attempts for this course in consideration for full admission to the Engineering major (excluding final letter grades of W, WP, and WF).

courses.description: This course introduces the fundamental and governing principles of systems of forces acting on rigid bodies, beams and columns as well as the analysis of truss, frame and machine structures. Topics include external and internal equilibrium of rigid bodies; systems of force and moment vectors; centroids; friction; loading that results in uniaxial, shear, flexure and torsion stresses and strains; and strength of materials. ENGR 212 and ENGR 212L must be taken concurrently.

courses.description: This course introduces the fundamentals of project management. Students will identify project requirements, develop a work breakdown structure and network diagram, and apply resources to develop a project schedule. Knowledge is demonstrated through proper application of the decision tools available to project managers, such as determining a project's current status for cost, schedule and performance. Students will analyze why a project's current status is not according to plan, develop an action plan to resolve cost and scheduling challenges, and project final cost, completion date and performance. A computer-based project management system is used for managing projects. Completion of this course fulfills the requirement for 23 formal education hours for the Certified Associate in Project Management (CAPM) credential.

Topics include understanding and detailing customer requirements, exploring the engineering solution space, down-selecting conceptual design solutions and developing low-fidelity prototypes. Additional topics include force analysis and equilibrium in the context of an interdisciplinary project experience. This course includes significant team and project-based components and provides opportunities to build interpersonal communication skills that lead to effective problem solving, idea generation, design embodiment and decision making. Students are permitted a maximum of two attempts for this course in consideration for full admission to the Engineering major (excluding final letter grades of W, WP, and WF).

courses.description: This course provides a comprehensive exploration of the science of literacy, focusing on how children and adolescents acquire and develop literacy skills across a variety of learners in K-12 classrooms. Grounded in evidence-based research, the course examines the cognitive and neurological processes involved in literacy development and acquisition, including an in-depth look at the reading brain and how it adapts to written language. Students will engage with foundational frameworks such as the Simple View of Reading, which emphasizes the dual importance of decoding and language comprehension, and will analyze the five pillars of literacy-phonemic awareness, phonics, fluency, vocabulary and comprehension. Additionally, the course will explore Scarborough's Reading Rope, illustrating the complex, interwoven strands that contribute to skilled reading. The course also emphasizes the role of assessment in guiding instruction and monitoring progress, equipping educators with tools to evaluate literacy skills effectively. By the end of the course, students will be prepared to apply scientifically grounded literacy practices to support all learners in achieving reading proficiency.

Assessment and instruction in social skills, sensory processing, communication and language development, and literacy instruction (including reading and writing) will be explored. A range of instructional methodologies and techniques for providing instruction, support and generalization of skills in these areas will be considered. This course will focus on the importance of relying on evidence-based practices and where to find information about EBPs.
